title: Problem 06
markdown:
### Problem
Show that the series

$$\sum_{k=1}^\infty \ln\left(1 + \frac{1}{k^2 + 2k}\right)$$

converges, and find its sum.

### Solution (adapted from the official solution)
### 1. Factor

$$
1 + \frac{1}{k^2 + 2k} = \frac{k(k+2) + 1}{k(k+2)}
$$

$$
= \frac{(k+1)^2}{k(k+2)}.
$$

### 2. Log

$$
\ln\left(\frac{(k+1)^2}{k(k+2)}\right) = 2\ln(k+1) - \ln k - \ln(k+2).
$$

### 3. Telescoping

$$
\sum_{k=1}^\infty \ln\left(1 + \frac{1}{k^2 + 2k}\right)
$$

$$
= \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{k=1}^n [2\ln(k+1) - \ln k - \ln(k+2)]
$$

$$
= \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{k=1}^n [(\ln(k+1) - \ln k) - (\ln(k+2) - \ln(k+1))]
$$

$$
= \lim_{n \to \infty} [\ln(n+1) - \ln 1 - \ln(n+2) + \ln 2]
$$

$$
= \ln 2 + \lim_{n \to \infty} \ln\left(\frac{n+1}{n+2}\right).
$$

### 4. Limit

$$
= \ln 2 + \lim_{n \to \infty} \ln\left(\frac{1 + \frac{1}{n}}{1 + \frac{2}{n}}\right)
$$

$$
= \ln 2 + \ln\left(\frac{1 + 0}{1 + 0}\right)
$$

$$
= \ln 2 + \ln 1
$$

$$
= \ln 2.
$$

$$
\therefore\ \text{The series converges to } \ln 2. \quad \blacksquare
$$

### Conceptual Explanation
Factoring the fractional argument into $\frac{(k+1)^2}{k(k+2)}$ splits each logarithmic term into $(\ln(k+1) - \ln k) - (\ln(k+2) - \ln(k+1))$ via [log laws](#node/node-exponents-and-logs/sec-exponents-and-logs-core). The partial sum telescopes to $\ln 2 + \ln\frac{n+1}{n+2}$, which converges to $\ln 2$ via [limits](#node/node-limits-foundation/sec-limits-core).

### Key Technique
[Telescoping logarithmic expansion](#node/node-telescoping-technique/sec-telescoping-core) $\ln\frac{(k+1)^2}{k(k+2)} = \Delta(\ln(k+1) - \ln k)$ using [log laws](#node/node-exponents-and-logs/sec-exponents-and-logs-core) and [series limits](#node/node-limits-foundation/sec-limits-core).
